q: You are rigging a snubber for a night at anchor in your 24 m yacht, with a swell running in. Your mate offers the line in the figure. What do you say?
a: No: it hardly stretches, so each snatch hits the fittings
o: Yes: twice the strength means half the risk of parting
Yes, if you double it so that it can never part
Yes, once each end has a good whipping on it
why: A snubber works by stretching; Dyneema stretches about 1%, so the shock loads go straight into the chain, cleats and windlass.

fig.title: The mate's offer for the snubber
lines: 14 mm Dyneema, spare halyard stock
“Twice as strong as our nylon”
Stretch at working load: about 1%

q: You are making up a towing bridle from 12 mm Dyneema for an offshore tow. Your crew starts tying a bowline in each end. What do you tell them?
a: Splice the eyes: knots slip in it and halve its strength
o: Carry on: Dyneema is strong enough for any knot
Carry on, but tape the tails flat along the line
Tie figure-of-eight loops, which hold in any rope
why: Dyneema is slippery and weak in knots: a bowline can creep out and keeps about half its strength; a spliced eye keeps most of it.

q: You read this note in the survey of your 20 m sloop before the season. What do you do about the runners?
a: Replace them: aramid weakens with flexing and UV, unseen
o: Keep them: aramid does not age the way polyester does
Turn them end for end and keep them for a season
Keep them and check the covers at mid-season
why: Aramid loses strength from flex fatigue over sheaves and from UV with no outward sign; old aramid running rigging is replaced on age.

fig.title: Survey before the season
lines: Running backstays: aramid core, 7 years
Cover clean, no chafe, no stiffness
Worked hard every season over 80 mm sheaves
Plan: 2,000 M offshore this summer

q: You are lengthening the rode of your 20 m yacht for a season of deep anchorages. Which rope and which join?
a: 8-plait nylon, spliced through the last chain link
o: Three-strand polyester, shackled to the last link
Dyneema braid, with a thimbled eye and a shackle
8-plait nylon, with a thimbled eye and a shackle
why: 8-plait nylon stretches and stows without kinking; a rope-to-chain splice runs over the gypsy, where a shackle and thimble jam.

fig.title: Lengthening the rode
lines: Windlass gypsy takes rope and 10 mm chain
50 m of chain now; adding 100 m of rope
The join must run over the gypsy

q: You will tie this line into the bridle with bowlines for a tow in a seaway. What is the most working load you should put on it?
a: About 0.6 t
o: About 1.0 t
About 3.1 t
About 0.7 t
why: 6.0 × 0.85 wet × 0.6 for the knot = 3.06 t at break; ÷ 5 = about 0.6 t.

fig.title: Line for the tow bridle
lines: 16 mm nylon three-strand, MBS 6.0 t new
Wet nylon keeps about 85% of that
A bowline keeps about 60% of the rest
Safety factor for towing: 5

q: You are buying new stern lines for a gale berth stern-to. What is the smallest size that does the job?
a: 28 mm
o: 24 mm
20 mm
36 mm
why: 3.0 t per line × 4 = 12 t; ÷ 0.9 for the splice = 13.3 t, so 28 mm (16.6 t). 24 mm forgets the splice.

fig.title: Gale berth, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Stern load 6.0 t, shared by two lines
Safety factor 4; eye splice keeps 90%
Nylon MBS: 20 mm 8.8 t · 24 mm 12.5 t

q: A surge is running into the harbour and you double up your bow lines like this. When the surge snatches, what share of the load does line A take?
a: About two-thirds of it
o: About half of it
About a third of it
All of it, until A parts
why: A line's stiffness goes as 1/length: the 6 m line is twice as stiff as the 12 m one, so it takes 2/3. Make doubled lines the same length.

fig.title: Doubling up for the surge
lines: Bow line A: 6 m from cleat to bollard
Bow line B: 12 m, to a farther bollard
Same nylon, both made just taut

q: You have cut new 24 mm three-strand mooring lines for the season. How do you finish the cut ends so they last?
a: A sailmaker's whipping, sewn through the strands
o: A heat-sealed end, melted with a hot knife
A common whipping of twine round the end
A few turns of tape, wound tight over the end
why: A sailmaker's or palm-and-needle whipping is stitched through the rope and cannot slide off; a melted end or tape soon frays.

q: You must join two lengths of 20 mm three-strand nylon into one long warp that has to run through a snatch block made for 20 mm rope. Which splice?
a: A long splice — it keeps the rope's diameter
o: A short splice — the strongest join of all
Two eye splices, joined with a shackle
A short splice, with its fat part tapered
why: A short splice nearly doubles the diameter and jams in the sheave; a long splice keeps the diameter, so it runs through the block.

q: The braid-on-braid main halyard of your 20 m sloop is furry and thin in the cover where it sits in the clutch at full hoist, but not worn through. What do you do?
a: Turn it end for end, moving the wear off the clutch
o: Nothing: the core carries all of the load
Tape over the worn part and keep it as it is
Strip the cover off and use the core alone
why: In braid-on-braid the cover takes part of the load and protects the core; end-for-ending puts fresh cover in the clutch.

q: You need to anchor for the night where the chart and the pilot book show this bottom. Which anchor do you use?
a: The fisherman — its thin fluke spears the kelp
o: The CQR — its plough digs in under the weed
The Bruce — its claw grips rock the best
The Danforth — its flukes bite the deepest
why: Broad flukes skate over kelp and rock; the fisherman's narrow arm gets through the weed and hooks a crevice.

fig.title: Anchorage in a Scottish sea loch
lines: Depth 9 m at the chosen spot
Seabed: rock under thick kelp
Aboard: CQR, Bruce, Danforth, fisherman

q: You anchor here for the night in your 20 m yacht. How do you lie?
a: To the Rocna: it turns and resets as she swings
o: To the Danforth: it holds the most in sand
To the Danforth, with extra chain for the veer
To both in a V, spread either side of the SW
why: A Danforth-type holds well in a straight pull but often trips and clogs when pulled round; a roll-bar anchor turns and resets.

fig.title: Anchoring before a cold front
lines: Sand, 6 m; wind SW 5 now
Front at 0300: veering NW 7
Aboard: Rocna-type 55 kg (bower)
and Danforth-type 30 kg (kedge)

q: The chain of your 24 m yacht is worn and the yard offers this replacement. What do you do?
a: Refuse it: buy chain made to fit the gypsy
o: Take it: the same 13 mm fits any gypsy
Take it: high-test chain is stronger, so better
Take it and run it with the clutch half on
why: A gypsy is cut for one chain's link pitch and width; chain to another standard rides up and jumps the gypsy under load.

fig.title: Replacing the chain
lines: Old: 13 mm, DIN 766, links worn
Yard offers 13 mm ISO 4565 (G4)
Windlass gypsy: DIN 766, 13 mm

q: You must ride out a gale at anchor here, with no tide to allow for. How much nylon do you let out after the chain?
a: About 60 m
o: About 46 m
About 20 m
About 140 m
why: (18 + 2) × 7 = 140 m of rode; less the 80 m of chain = 60 m of nylon.
ref: Anchoring — scope by depth and weather

fig.title: Open roadstead, gale tonight
lines: 80 m of chain, then nylon
Bow roller 2 m above water
Chain and rope: 7:1 tonight

q: You are checking whether the windlass of your 24 m yacht can weigh the anchor here. What pull does it need?
a: About 440 kg
o: About 260 kg
About 150 kg
About 950 kg
why: 60 + 27 × 3.2 = 146 kg lifted; × 3 = about 440 kg. Only the hanging chain counts, not all 80 m.

fig.title: Weighing anchor in 25 m
lines: Anchor 60 kg; 80 m of 12 mm chain out
Chain 3.2 kg/m; 27 m hangs as it lifts
Windlass pull: 3 × the weight lifted

q: You must ride out this gale at anchor in the lee of the shore, with good sand and plenty of room. How do you lay two anchors?
a: Both ahead in a V: one to the SW, one to the W
o: One to the SW and one to the NE, 180° apart
Both let go together, close under the bow
One to the SE and one to the SW, 90° apart
why: An open moor spreads two anchors ahead across the expected wind, so both share the load as it veers; 180° apart is for a reversing stream.

fig.note: Gale SW 8 for 24 h, veering W

q: You will lie to a Bahamian moor for five days in a tidal river. How do you stop the two rodes twisting round each other?
a: Join both to a mooring swivel lowered below the keel
o: Lead both rodes over the same bow roller
Lay the two anchors 90° apart, not 180°
Make both rodes fast on the same bow cleat
why: She turns with every tide, wrapping the rodes; a swivel joining them below the keel lets her turn without twisting them.

q: What do you do to stop her sheering about at anchor?
a: Set a small riding sail on the mizzen
o: Let out all the remaining chain
Run the engine slow ahead all night
Shorten the chain to hold her tighter
why: A riding sail aft acts like a weathervane, holding her head to wind so she stops sheering and snatching.

fig.title: At anchor: ketch, F6 gusting 8
lines: She sheers 40° each way in the gusts
Chain snatches at the end of each sheer
Plenty of chain out, anchor holding

q: You are preparing your 24 m yacht for offshore anchorages. How should the bitter end of the chain be secured in the locker?
a: By a lashing you can cut, long enough to reach the deck
o: By a shackle to an eye, moused with wire
By welding it to the bottom of the locker
Not at all: the chain's weight holds it
why: If the windlass fails while she drags, you must be able to slip the chain: a lashing can be cut, and a buoy on the end marks it.

q: You have touched on this bank and will lay the kedge out into deep water with the tender. How do you do it?
a: Anchor and warp in the tender, warp paid out as you go
o: Warp paid out from the yacht, towed behind the tender
Anchor laid first, the warp brought on a second trip
Warp in the tender, the anchor towed along behind it
why: Pay the warp out from the tender as you go, so you never drag its weight through the water; drop the anchor at full length.

q: You are on a 140 M passage and decide to anchor here until daylight. How do you go in?
a: Slowly on radar and sounder; anchor on the 10 m contour
o: Into the inner cove, where the shelter is best
Along another yacht's plotter track into the cove
Not in at all: anchor outside in 30 m, well clear
why: In the dark trust what you can measure: radar ranges and the contour lead to charted sand; close in on an old survey is no place at night.
ref: Anchoring — at night on a strange coast

fig.title: 0200, off an unlit bay
lines: Crew tired after 30 h; wind W 4 offshore
Bay mouth: sand, the 10 m contour across it
Inner cove 3 m: rocks, old survey
Radar, sounder and plotter all working

q: At least how far from her anchor do you drop yours, so that your swinging circles can never meet?
a: About 140 m
o: About 85 m
About 100 m
About 275 m
why: Each radius is the chain's run plus the boat: √(60² − 12²) + 24 ≈ 83 m and √(45² − 11²) + 12 ≈ 56 m; together about 140 m.

fig.title: Anchoring near another yacht
lines: You: 24 m motor yacht, 60 m of chain
Her: 12 m sloop, 45 m of chain
Depth 10 m; rollers 2 m (you), 1 m (her)
Wind against tide: you will lie differently

q: You are anchoring in this Croatian channel. How do you lower the anchor?
a: Under power, all the way to the bottom
o: In free fall, braked hard as it touches
In free fall, stopped halfway down
In free fall, with the engines astern
why: In deep water a free-falling anchor and chain gather speed the brake may not hold, and the chain piles on the anchor; power it down.

fig.title: Deep water, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Hydraulic windlass, band brake
70 kg anchor, 13 mm chain

q: You are writing the anchor-watch orders for tonight. How should the watch check the anchor?
a: Radar range and bearing every 15 min, logged, and the alarm
o: The GPS alarm alone — it covers the whole circle
A torch on the beach ahead, checked now and then
The chain, felt by hand at the bow each half hour
why: With nothing lit ashore, a logged radar range and EBL to the headland plus the GPS alarm show dragging early, even as she swings.

fig.title: Anchor watch 0100, shore unlit
lines: Headland 0.9 M on radar, bearing 040°T
GPS alarm set on the anchor, 90 m radius
Front due 0300: wind veering 90°

q: Your 22 m motor yacht lies parallel to the pontoon, 4 m off it to starboard. How do you walk her sideways onto it?
a: Thruster to starboard; starboard engine ahead, port astern
o: Thruster to starboard; port engine ahead, starboard astern
Thruster to port; starboard engine ahead, port astern
Thruster to starboard; both engines slow ahead
why: Starboard ahead and port astern swing the stern to starboard; the thruster pushes the bow the same way, so she moves bodily sideways.

fig.note: Twin screws, bow thruster · pontoon to starboard

q: From rest, you put only the port engine astern, with the starboard one in neutral. What does the stern do?
a: Swings to starboard — offset and prop walk add up
o: Swings to port — the prop walk beats the offset
Goes straight back — the two effects cancel
Swings to port — as in any boat going astern
why: The port shaft's pull aft swings the stern to starboard, and its left-handed prop going astern kicks the stern to starboard too.

fig.note: Props turn outwards · port engine astern only

q: Your 22 m motor yacht is pinned to this quay with a yacht close ahead. You want to leave bow first. How do you get the bow out?
a: Stern spring on, fender aft, port engine astern
o: Stern spring on, fender aft, starboard engine astern
Bow spring on, fender forward, port engine ahead
Stern spring on, fender aft, both engines ahead
why: Going astern on the stern spring holds the quarter and swings the bow out; the outboard (port) engine astern adds to it.

fig.note: Twin screws · wind E 5, onto the quay

q: Your 20 m yacht lies alongside this Breton harbour wall for the evening. How much slack must each spring have at HW so it is not bar-taut by LW?
a: About 0.8 m
o: About 5.0 m
About 1.7 m
About 15.8 m
why: At LW the spring runs 15 m along and 5 m down: √(15² + 5²) = 15.8 m, 0.8 m more than at HW. Short lines need far more.

fig.title: Alongside a wall, range 5.0 m
lines: At HW the bollards are level with the deck
Springs: 15 m from cleat to bollard
You will be ashore from HW until LW

q: You must lie alongside a jetty of wide-spaced timber piles in a swell. Your fenders keep rolling into the gaps. What do you rig?
a: A fender board hung outside the fenders
o: More fenders, tied closer together
Fenders laid flat along the topsides
Breast lines hauled in bar-tight
why: A plank outside the fenders bridges the piles, so the fenders stay put and press on the board, not into the gaps.

q: Your 24 m yacht is the inside boat of a raft on the town quay. Three more yachts — 11 m, 18 m and 14 m — want to raft out. In what order should they come?
a: 18 m, then 14 m, then 11 m outside
o: 11 m, then 14 m, then 18 m outside
In order of arrival, whatever their size
14 m, then 11 m, then 18 m outside
why: Biggest inside to smallest outside, so each boat's lines and fenders hold a smaller boat, never a larger one.

q: You are stern-to on your own anchor and the passerelle is grinding on the quay. What do you change?
a: Cross the stern lines: port quarter to starboard bollard
o: Haul both stern lines in until the stern touches
Add a third line straight back from the centre
Ease the anchor chain so she lies more freely
why: Crossed lines are longer and pull across as well as aft, so they check the sideways swing; the passerelle stays clear of the quay.

fig.title: Stern-to, 24 m yacht
lines: Wind on the beam, gusting 25 kn
Stern lines run straight back to the bollards
Stern swings 1.5 m sideways in each gust

q: Your mate wants to lay your own anchor as well, to be safe tonight. What do you decide?
a: No: it fouls the ground chains; double the lazy lines
o: Yes: lay it ahead to share the lazy lines' load
Yes, but only if the wind really reaches F7
No, but ease the lazy lines so she rides easier
why: Where lazy lines are laid, an anchor hooks the ground chains; put both lazy lines on, tight and with chafe gear, and tend them.

fig.title: Marina berth, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Two lazy lines laid to your berth
Ground chains run across the basin
Meltemi forecast F7 on the beam tonight

q: You are going astern into this slot from rest. What will she try to do, and how do you counter it?
a: Bow falls to starboard; thruster to port, sternway early
o: Bow falls to port; thruster to starboard, go slowly
She tracks straight — wind and prop walk cancel
Stern swings to starboard; port helm on early
why: A right-handed prop kicks the stern to port going astern, and the wind on the port beam blows the bow to starboard: both turn her one way.
ref: Boat handling — prop walk and wind

fig.note: 20 m sloop, one RH prop · wind W 5

q: You are to moor fore-and-aft between these two piles in a Solent river. How do you make the approach?
a: Head west into the ebb; bow line to the west pile first
o: Head east with the ebb; bow line to the east pile first
Head west into the ebb; stern line to the east pile first
Head east with the ebb; stern line to the west pile first
why: Stem the stream for control, make the bow fast to the up-tide pile first, then drop back on it and take the stern line to the other.

fig.note: Fore-and-aft between piles · ebb 2 kn E

q: You are towing a dismasted yacht home. How much towline do you let out?
a: About 100 m
o: About 50 m
About 12 m
About 150 m
why: 1.56 × 8² ≈ 100 m: one wave length keeps both boats on the same part of a wave; at 50 or 150 m one is on a crest, one in a trough.

fig.title: Tow 80 M offshore, a long swell
lines: Swell period 8 s, from astern
Deep-water wave length ≈ 1.56 × T² m
Towline aboard: 150 m of 24 mm nylon

q: You are towing this yacht towards the harbour entrance over the bar. What do you do before you reach it?
a: Shorten the tow, for control and to keep the bight off the bottom
o: Keep 100 m out — the longer tow is always the safer
Let out more line so that the catenary is deeper
Speed up so that the line lifts clear of the water
why: A long catenary can drag on a shallow bar and gives no control in a narrow entrance; shorten up in sheltered water, then go alongside.

q: You are taking a disabled yacht in tow offshore with your 20 m yacht. How do you make the towline fast on board?
a: Turns round a strong central point, to ease or cut at will
o: Shackled to the stern cleat, so it can never slip
A bowline round a primary winch, tied off hard
Round the pushpit, to keep it clear of the rudder
why: Under load you may need to ease or slip the tow at once: turns on a strong central post can be surged, with a knife kept beside it.

q: You are about to take another yacht in tow at dusk, 40 M offshore. What do you agree with her skipper first?
a: A VHF channel, the speed, and the signals to slow or stop
o: Only who pays for the tow, before anything else
Nothing: the tow simply follows the towing boat
A VHF channel; the rest can be sorted as you go
why: Agree a working channel, the towing speed and back-up signals (torch, horn) for slow, stop and let go before the line takes the strain.

q: What lights do you show at night while you tow her?
a: Three masthead lights in a line, towing light, sides, stern
o: Two masthead lights in a line, towing light, sides, stern
One masthead light, towing light, sidelights, sternlight
Two masthead lights in a line, sidelights, sternlight only
why: The length of tow runs from your stern to her stern: 195 + 12 = 207 m, over 200 m, so three masthead lights; a diamond by day too.

fig.title: Night tow, under power
lines: Your yacht: 20 m, motoring
Towline 195 m from your stern to her bow
The towed yacht is 12 m long

q: You are towing this yacht alongside into the marina. Which line takes the load when you go ahead?
a: The spring led aft from your bow to her quarter
o: The spring led forward from your quarter to her bow
The bow line between your two bows
The stern line between your two sterns
why: Going ahead you move forward against her, so the line leading aft from your bow tightens; going astern the forward-led spring takes it.

fig.title: Towing alongside into the marina
lines: She lies on your port side
Your stern well aft of hers
Bow line, stern line and two springs on

q: You leave at dusk for a 130 M crossing with the RIB tender you have towed between anchorages all week. What do you do with it?
a: Lift it aboard and lash it down for the crossing
o: Tow it on a long painter, riding on a wave
Tow it on a short painter, close up astern
Tow it on two painters, the outboard aboard
why: Offshore a towed tender can swamp, flip or part its painters, and at night it is a hazard astern; stow it on deck or on the davits.

q: You are being towed home overnight by a fishing boat. What do you do about the towline at your bow?
a: Check it hourly and ease it a little to freshen the nip
o: Leave it alone — the chafe guard will last all night
Make it fast tighter, so it can no longer move
Lead it over the pulpit, away from the roller
why: However good the guard, one spot wears through; easing the line a little each hour moves the wear to fresh rope.

fig.title: Being towed, 10 h to go
lines: Towline over your bow roller
Chafe guard fitted at the start
The line saws on the roller as she pitches

q: In a F9 with breaking seas, a crew member suggests taking all sail down and letting your 20 m yacht lie a-hull for a rest. What do you say?
a: No: lying beam-on to breaking seas risks a knockdown
o: Yes: with no sail up she cannot be knocked down
Yes: a big yacht lies a-hull safely in any sea
Yes, once the helm is lashed hard to windward
why: A-hull she lies beam-on, and a breaking crest about her beam in height can roll her. Heave to, or run with a drogue.

q: You heave to in your 20 m sloop to wait for daylight, but she forereaches at 3 kn and lies almost beam-on. What do you do?
a: Ease the main further and lash the helm harder to leeward
o: Sheet the main in hard, so that she points higher
Let the backed jib fly, so it stops driving her
Run the engine slow ahead to hold her head up
why: Forereaching means the main is driving: ease it and add lee helm, so she lies 50° off the wind and drifts, leaving a slick to windward.

fig.note: Hove-to: forereaching at 3 kn, nearly beam-on

q: You have chosen to run off before this gale. What do you do now?
a: Stream a drogue on a bridle from both quarters
o: Turn beam-on and lie a-hull until it eases
Bear away dead downwind and set more sail
Stream the drogue from the bow, head to sea
why: A drogue astern slows her to a speed you can steer and holds the stern to the seas; a bridle to both quarters keeps the pull central.

fig.title: Running before a gale, F9
lines: Surfing at 14 kn down the faces
Two near-broaches in the last hour
Sea room downwind: 200 M

q: Your 20 m yacht must ride out this gale. Which tactic keeps her off the shore?
a: Lie to the parachute sea anchor from the bow
o: Heave to under the trysail and storm jib
Run off under bare poles, steering by hand
Run off slowly, towing the drogue astern
why: In 18 h: 5 kn → 90 M, 3 kn → 54 M, 2 kn → 36 M, all past the 30 M shore; 1 kn → 18 M leaves 12 M in hand.

fig.title: Gale for 18 h, lee shore 30 M
lines: No way can be made to windward
Drift: bare poles 5 kn · drogue 3 kn
Hove-to 2 kn · parachute sea anchor 1 kn

q: You are setting the trysail in your 20 m sloop for a gale offshore. How is it rigged?
a: On its own mast track, sheeted to the quarters, boom lashed
o: On the main track, sheeted to the end of the boom
Set flying from a halyard, its tack at the bow
On the main track, its clew lashed to the boom
why: A trysail goes up a separate track over the stowed main and sheets to the quarters, so the boom can be lashed down out of the way.

q: Before a 140 M crossing with a gale possible on the second day, how do you prepare the storm jib?
a: Hank it on the inner forestay and hoist it once in harbour
o: Leave it bagged in the forepeak until it is needed
Plan to set it round the furled genoa at sea
Plan to roll the genoa down to its size instead
why: Rig and try storm sails before you go: on an inner forestay the storm jib sets low and inboard; set at sea for the first time, it often fails.

q: You will lie to a parachute sea anchor through the night. How do you rig it?
a: From the bow on long nylon, with chafe gear at the roller
o: From the stern, so that she drifts more slowly
From the bow on a short rode, to hold her tight
From the bow on Dyneema, so the rode never stretches
why: The parachute holds the bow to the seas; a long, stretchy nylon rode absorbs the snatch, and the chafe point is guarded.

q: You must keep heading for port in these seas. How do you drive her?
a: Slow to displacement speed, seas 20–30° on the bow
o: Keep planing, to be in port before it worsens
Slow to displacement speed, seas dead ahead
Turn beam-on between seas and wait for a lull
why: Off the plane she rides the seas without slamming; taking them a little on the bow eases the pitching and keeps her steering.

fig.title: 24 m planing motor yacht, F8
lines: Head seas 4 m, short and steep
At 22 kn she is slamming hard
Port 60 M upwind

q: You are making a soft eye in 10 mm 12-strand Dyneema for a tow pennant. Your crew, used to polyester three-strand, starts to unlay it for tucks. What splice do you tell them to make?
a: A locked bury splice with a long, tapered tail
o: Four tucks, as they would make in polyester
A short bury, the tail melted to lock it in
Tucks through the braid, each sealed by heat
why: Dyneema is too slippery to hold short tucks: the tail is tapered and buried a long way inside the hollow braid, and heat only weakens it.

fig.title: Splicing the tow pennant
lines: 10 mm 12-strand Dyneema, a hollow braid
Very slippery; melts at about 150 °C
Crew's habit: tucked splices in polyester

q: You are eye-splicing a new length of three-strand nylon for a storm snubber. How many tucks do you make?
a: At least five full tucks, then taper the tails
o: Three tucks, as for a natural-fibre rope
Two tucks, then heat-seal the strands
Three tucks, with a whipping over them
why: Nylon is slippery and stretches, so a splice needs at least five full tucks to hold; fewer can draw out under repeated load.

q: You are refitting your 22 m yacht for an offshore season and can replace only one set of lines now. Which do you replace?
a: The nylon dock lines: hard, stiff nylon has lost much strength
o: The polyester sheets: any fuzz means the cover is finished
The Dyneema halyards: Dyneema ages fastest of the four
The snubber: nylon must be renewed every two years
why: Sun, salt crystals and years of cyclic loading break nylon down from inside; stiff, faded nylon has lost a large part of its strength.

fig.title: Lines at the end of last season
lines: Nylon dock lines, 6 yrs: hard, stiff, faded
Polyester sheets, 6 yrs: supple, a little fuzzy
Dyneema-core halyards, 3 yrs: covers sound
Nylon snubber, 2 yrs: supple, slight chafe

q: Three hours into the tow, you check the pennant at your stern fairlead. What is happening, and what do you do?
a: Friction is melting it: shift the nip and keep it cool
o: Normal wear: Dyneema shrugs off any chafe
Sun damage from the day: tape over the spot
Salt crystals: rinse it in fresh water later
why: Dyneema weakens when hot and melts near 150 °C; a glossy, hard patch at a hot fairlead is friction heat: move the nip, wet it, or re-lead.

fig.title: Towing, 3 h in
lines: Pennant: 12 mm Dyneema through a steel fairlead
It saws 10 cm to and fro as she pitches
Fairlead hot; rope glossy and hard there

q: You are towing on a bridle from both quarters. What load does each leg carry?
a: About 1.1 t
o: About 0.8 t
About 1.6 t
About 2.3 t
why: Each leg = 1.6 ÷ (2 × cos 45°) ≈ 1.1 t: the wider the bridle, the more each leg carries above half the pull.

fig.title: Towing bridle
lines: Legs from both quarters to a ring
Angle between the legs at the ring: 90°
Steady pull on the towline: 1.6 t

q: You must join two 24 mm nylon warps end to end for a long tow, with no time to splice, and untie them in port afterwards. Which bend?
a: A carrick bend, its ends seized to the standing parts
o: A reef knot, pulled up hard and taped
A single sheet bend, as the warps match
A double fisherman's knot, pulled up hard
why: A seized carrick bend holds heavy warps and still comes undone after a hard load; a reef knot capsizes, and a fisherman's jams solid.

q: You are coiling a new right-hand-laid three-strand warp to stow in the lazarette. Which way do you coil it?
a: Clockwise, with the lay
o: Anticlockwise, against the lay
Clockwise and anticlockwise in turn
Round hand and elbow, as it comes
why: Right-hand-laid rope is coiled clockwise; coiled the other way, each turn adds twist and the warp kinks when it runs out.

q: Your tow bridle's spliced eye goes straight over the pin of a shackle on the towing ring. About what load will break it there?
a: About 4.9 t
o: About 8.1 t
About 5.4 t
About 9.0 t
why: 9.0 × 0.9 × 0.6 ≈ 4.9 t: a tight bend over a thin pin costs more than the splice. A thimble or a fat pin keeps much more.

fig.title: Bridle eye on a shackle
lines: 12 mm Dyneema, MBS 9.0 t new
Eye splice keeps about 90%
Over a 24 mm pin (D/d 2): about 60% kept

q: After a night of surge in the harbour, the bowline in the end of your nylon stern line has half shaken loose. What do you do?
a: Replace it with a spliced eye that cannot work loose
o: Retie it pulled hard: a bowline never shakes loose
Replace it with a clove hitch over the bollard
Replace it with a reef knot round the bollard
why: A bowline can loosen when the load comes on and off again and again, as in a surge; a spliced eye cannot work loose.

q: You must lie to one anchor in this muddy estuary through tonight's gale. Which anchor do you lay?
a: The 32 kg Danforth: about 960 kg
o: The 55 kg Rocna: about 2,750 kg
The 40 kg Delta: about 1,400 kg
The 55 kg Rocna: about 1,650 kg
why: In mud: Rocna 55 × 12 = 660, Delta 40 × 5 = 200, Danforth 32 × 30 = 960 kg. Only the Danforth's wide flukes hold 900 kg there.

fig.title: Soft mud, gale load 900 kg
lines: Holding per kg of anchor, sand · mud:
Rocna 50 · 12 — aboard 55 kg
Delta 35 · 5 — aboard 40 kg
Danforth 40 · 30 — aboard 32 kg

q: Your Danforth-type kedge dragged on its first try here. What do you do?
a: Lay the heavy bower instead, and load it gently
o: Clear the pebble and drop the kedge again
Drop the kedge again, faster, to drive it in
Leave the pebble in, as weight to help it dig
why: Light flukes jam on stones and skid over shingle; a heavy anchor with a sharp point gets in, if you load it gradually.

fig.title: Off a shingle beach
lines: Seabed: shingle and pebbles, 7 m
Kedge dragged: a pebble jammed in its flukes
Bower aboard: a 45 kg plough

q: You are anchoring for lunch in this Balearic bay. Where do you drop the anchor?
a: In a pale sand patch, then look or dive to check it set
o: On the dark weed, where it is thickest, for holding
Anywhere: weed matters only for small anchors
On the weed, with extra chain to drag it through
why: Anchors skate over sea-grass, and here it is protected too; drop in clear sand, where the anchor digs, and check it with a look or a dive.

fig.title: Balearic bay, clear water, 8 m
lines: Chart: Wd over S
Local rules: no anchoring on sea-grass
Pale sand patches between dark weed

q: You are staying two nights here. How do you rig the chain to stop this?
a: Float its middle on a buoy, so it lifts clear of the rocks
o: Shorten it, so that less of it can wrap round
Change to the nylon rode, which slides over rock
Let all of it out, so that it lies flat over them
why: A buoy part way along lifts the chain clear of the rocks, so it cannot wrap and shorten itself; nylon dragged over rock chafes through.

fig.title: Anchored over boulders, 12 m
lines: Sand pockets between big rocks
Light wind, shifting all night
Chain grinds and snatches: it has wrapped a rock

q: You are choosing new chain for your 24 m yacht. What is the smallest size that does the job?
a: 16 mm
o: 13 mm
12 mm
10 mm
why: 2.1 × 4 = 8.4 t; ÷ 0.8 for wear = 10.5 t: 16 mm. The snubber takes it to the bow, but the chain still carries the whole load.

fig.title: 24 m yacht: choosing the chain
lines: Storm load 2.1 t, on a two-leg snubber
Chain: × 4 on its break; 80% left when worn
Break: 10 mm 5.0 t · 12 mm 7.2 t · 13 mm 8.5 t

q: You want the gale's pull to stay horizontal at the anchor, so it cannot lift the shank. How much chain must be out?
a: About 114 m
o: About 98 m
About 106 m
About 81 m
why: h = 14 m; 1,500 ÷ 3.3 ≈ 455 m; √(14 × (14 + 909)) ≈ 114 m. Use the chain's weight in water, and the catenary, not 7:1.

fig.title: Exposed roadstead, gale tonight
lines: Depth 12 m; bow roller 2 m up: h = 14 m
13 mm chain: 3.8 kg/m in air, 3.3 in water
Gale pull at the bow: about 1,500 kg
Least chain = √(h × (h + 2 × pull ÷ weight))

q: You are anchored in this open roadstead at 1600. What do you decide?
a: Weigh and get to sea before dark, while you still can
o: Stay, and add all the nylon rode to the chain
Stay, and lay the kedge in tandem with the bower
Stay, and run the engines slow ahead all night
why: An onshore gale makes a roadstead a lee shore: if she drags at night there is no room to recover. Sea room is safer than any extra gear.

fig.title: Open roadstead, 1600
lines: Gale SW 8 from 2200, onshore
Rocks 0.3 M astern; 100 m of chain out
Swell already 2 m and building

q: You will lay a Bahamian moor here, stemming the flood, with 40 m of chain on each anchor. How do you lay it?
a: First anchor, drop back 80 m, second anchor, heave back to the middle
o: Both anchors together, then drop back on both chains
First anchor, drop back 40 m, second anchor, stay there
First anchor, then the second across the river from it
why: Let go the up-stream anchor, drop back twice the scope, let go the second, then heave in on the first: she lies midway, 40 m to each.

fig.note: Bahamian moor · 40 m of chain on each

q: You lie to a Bahamian moor, riding to the up-stream anchor with the other chain slack. You are leaving. Which anchor do you weigh first?
a: The slack down-stream one, then the one she rides to
o: The one she rides to, then drop back for the other
Both together, heaving each chain in by turns
The up-stream one, as it holds the heavier load
why: Weigh the slack anchor while she still lies to the other; lift the riding one first and she drifts down over the second chain.

q: A strong wind blows straight across the river. How far off the line of the anchors can your stern be blown?
a: About 41 m
o: About 65 m
About 25 m
About 80 m
why: Both legs taut: √(45² − 40²) ≈ 21 m sideways for the swivel, plus 20 m of yacht downwind of it = about 41 m.
ref: Anchoring — two anchors in a river

fig.title: Bahamian moor in a river
lines: Anchors 80 m apart, along the stream
Each leg reaches 45 m from anchor to swivel
Yacht: 20 m from the swivel to her stern

q: You have hooked the nylon snubber onto the chain and made it fast. How much chain do you then let out?
a: Enough to hang in a slack loop below the hook
o: None: keep the chain taut to share the load
Just enough to bring the chain level with the hook
All the rest, so that it piles up on the anchor
why: The slack loop means the snubber carries the load and stretches; if the chain is taut, the shocks go straight back to the windlass.

fig.title: Snubber rigged, F6 tonight
lines: Snubber on a chain hook
Made fast to both bow cleats

q: Your 24 m motor yacht is sheering wildly at anchor. What do you do?
a: Drop the second anchor under the bow on a short chain
o: Shorten the bower's chain to hold her tighter
Run one engine slow ahead to steady her
Rig a riding sail on the bow to hold her head
why: A second anchor under foot, on chain a little longer than the depth, drags as she sheers and damps it; a sail forward only makes it worse.

fig.title: 24 m motor yacht at anchor, F7 gusts
lines: High bow and flybridge catch the wind
She sheers 60° each way, then snatches
Bower holding; second anchor ready

q: You ran onto this bank on the falling tide, and the wind is pushing her further onto it. When do you lay out the kedge?
a: Now, into deep water to windward, taking up slack as she lifts
o: Once she floats, so that the warp does not sit slack
Now, under the bow, on a short warp to steady her
Not at all: back her off on the engine as she floats
why: As she lifts the wind will drive her further up the bank; a kedge laid to windward now holds her, and you heave in as the tide comes.

q: You check the plotter's anchor track at 0200. What does it tell you?
a: She has dragged since the shift: re-anchor now
o: She is swinging to the new wind, as she should
The GPS has drifted, so the track means nothing
The chain is still straightening: let it settle
why: Swinging draws an arc about the anchor; a straight run downwind after the shift means the anchor broke out and she is dragging.

fig.title: Anchor track since 2200
lines: 2200–0130: an arc round the anchor, 70 m out
0130: the wind veers 100° in a squall
0130–0200: a straight line, 60 m downwind

q: You are about to back your 24 m motor yacht stern-to in this crosswind. Can the bow thruster alone hold her bow up to windward?
a: No: in the gusts the bow takes about 270 kgf
o: Yes: the mean wind puts about 160 kgf on it
Yes: in the gusts the bow takes about 10 kgf
No: in the gusts the bow takes about 540 kgf
why: 26² ÷ 60 × 24 m² ≈ 270 kgf on the bow in a gust, against a 160 kgf thruster; it is the gust, not the mean wind, you must hold.

fig.title: Stern-to in a crosswind
lines: Wind 20 kn, gusts 26, on the beam
Side windage 48 m², half of it on the bow
Wind load ≈ V² ÷ 60 kgf per m² (V in kn)
Bow thruster: 160 kgf

q: Your bow thruster cannot hold the bow in these gusts. How do you go stern-to in your 24 m motor yacht?
a: Anchor upwind, back in on the engines, brake the chain to hold the bow
o: Anchor dead ahead, chain free, hold the bow up on the thruster
Anchor downwind, chain free, let the wind lay her into the slot
No anchor: back in fast and get both stern lines on at once
why: The chain, snubbed as she backs in, holds the bow up to windward where the thruster cannot; the engines steer the stern into the slot.

fig.title: Stern-to, 24 m motor yacht
lines: Wind 20 kn gusting 26 across the berth
Slot between two yachts, quay astern
Thruster: too weak for the gusts

q: You expect a long, fiddly berthing in a gusty crosswind. How do you plan to use the bow thruster?
a: Short bursts at the key moments; chain and engines hold her
o: Steadily: the cut-out is there only for emergencies
Non-stop: it has its own battery to draw on
All the way in, then rest it once she is tied up
why: A thruster that cuts out halfway through the manoeuvre leaves the bow to the wind; save it for short bursts, and hold her on chain and engines.

fig.title: Bow thruster: maker's notes
lines: Electric, 7 kW, on its own battery
Run time 3 min, then a thermal cut-out
Cool enough to restart after about 15 min

q: You are stemming this stream in your 23 m twin-screw yacht, stopped over the ground 5 m off your gap on the quay. How do you close the last 5 m?
a: Both ahead to hold the stream, bow angled in a little
o: Walk her sideways on split engines and thruster
Both to neutral, and let the crew heave her in
Thruster towards the quay, both slow astern
why: Split engines give little or no thrust ahead, so the stream carries her back; held on both engines, bow angled in, the stream ferries her across.
ref: Twin screws — docking in a stream

fig.note: Twin screws · stopped over the ground, 5 m off

q: You are heading downstream to this berth on the quay, and the river is too narrow to turn your 23 m twin-screw yacht. How do you come alongside?
a: Pass the berth, stop, then back up to it against the stream
o: Come in bow first with the stream, stopping on the engines
Come in fast with the stream, to keep good steering way
Drift down beam-on to the stream and land her bodily
why: Going astern into the stream she is stemming it, slow over the ground and under control; with the stream behind her she cannot stop.
ref: Twin screws — docking in a stream

fig.note: River 1.2 lengths wide · 23 m, twin screws

q: You must leave at 0600. How do you get your 24 m yacht out of this raft?
a: The outer boats cast off and stand clear; then they re-raft
o: Spring the stern out with the whole raft still on you
Leave ahead and let the outer boats swing in behind
Go hard astern and slide out from under the raft
why: With the wind onto the quay the whole raft lies on you, and no spring or engine can move it; the outer boats must stand off while you leave.

fig.title: Raft on a tideless quay
lines: You: the inside boat, 24 m
Three yachts of 12–15 m outside you
Wind F5 onto the quay; crews aboard

q: You will tow this yacht 70 M to port through a moderate sea. What is the fastest you should tow her?
a: About 5.1 kn
o: About 5.9 kn
About 2.8 kn
About 7.7 kn
why: 10.0 m = 32.8 ft; 1.34 × √32.8 ≈ 7.7 kn hull speed; 2/3 of it ≈ 5.1 kn. Use the waterline length, not the overall length.

fig.title: Disabled sloop in tow
lines: LOA 13.4 m, LWL 10.0 m
Hull speed ≈ 1.34 × √LWL ft; 1 m = 3.28 ft
In a seaway: no more than 2/3 of it

q: You hang chain in the middle of the towline to give it spring. Under a steady pull, how deep does it hold the middle of the line?
a: About 1.4 m
o: About 1.7 m
About 0.7 m
About 5.7 m
why: 17 × 100 ÷ (4 × 300) ≈ 1.4 m: under a hard pull the weight soon lifts; the nylon's stretch, not the dip, is the real spring.

fig.title: Chain weight on the towline
lines: 100 m of nylon; steady pull 300 kg
20 kg of chain at its middle (17 kg in water)
Dip at the middle ≈ weight × length ÷ (4 × pull)

q: Your gearbox has failed 90 M offshore, and this ship will tow your 20 m sloop. How do you make her towline fast?
a: Spread over the mast foot and both bow cleats, guarded
o: Round the windlass, with its chain brake hard on
To one bow cleat alone, with a round turn on it
Round the pulpit base, to keep it off the anchor
why: A ship's pull can rip out a single cleat or a windlass; share it between the keel-stepped mast and both cleats, with chafe gear at the fairlead.
ref: Towing — being towed by a ship

fig.title: Taking a tow from a ship
lines: 70 m offshore supply ship
She passes over a heavy 48 mm towline
Your sloop: keel-stepped mast, two bow cleats

q: The trawler's skipper wants to get you to port quickly. What do you tell him?
a: No more than about 5 kn: near hull speed the loads soar
o: 8 kn is fine: it is still under her hull speed
As fast as he likes: the faster, the shorter the strain
8 kn is fine, as long as you steer straight behind
why: Towed near her hull speed a yacht squats, sheers and loads her fittings far harder; ask for well under it, however long it takes.
ref: Towing — being towed by a larger vessel

fig.title: Being towed by a trawler
lines: 30 m trawler; 50 M to port
He proposes 8 kn
Your yacht's hull speed: about 8.5 kn

q: You are being towed overnight. What does your helmsman do?
a: Steers all the time, keeping her in the towing boat's wake
o: Lashes the helm amidships and keeps a lookout
Leaves it to the autopilot on a fixed heading
Steers only when she sheers more than 30°
why: Unsteered, a tow sheers about and snatches the line; steered in the wake, she keeps the pull straight and the load even.

q: You are towing this yacht under power at night. What lights do the two vessels show?
a: You: two masthead, sides, stern, towing light · she: sides, stern
o: You: two masthead, sides, stern · she: sides, stern, towing light
You: one masthead, sides, stern, towing light · she: sides, stern
You: two masthead, sides, stern, towing light · she: masthead, sides, stern
why: Tow 110 + 10 = 120 m, under 200 m: two masthead lights, sidelights, sternlight and the yellow towing light; the tow shows sides and stern.

fig.title: Night tow
lines: You: 18 m motor yacht
Towline 110 m from your stern to her bow
She: a 10 m sailing yacht, no engine

q: You take a disabled yacht in tow at dusk, motoring. Your yacht has no towing lights. What do you show?
a: Steaming light, sides and stern, a searchlight on the towline
o: The tricolour only, as you have no towing lights
Your anchor light, to show that you are slow
Tricolour and steaming light, a torch on deck
why: Rule 24(i): a vessel not normally towing that helps one in need may omit the towing lights, but must show the tow, as by lighting the towline.

fig.title: Your 20 m sailing yacht
lines: Lights: tricolour, steaming light
Deck-level sidelights and sternlight
No second masthead light, no towing light

q: You are towing by day, with 220 m from your stern to the stern of the tow. What shapes are shown?
a: A diamond on each vessel, where best seen
o: A diamond on the tow only, aft
A diamond on your yacht only
A black ball on each vessel
why: Rule 24: when the tow is over 200 m long, the towing vessel and the tow each show a diamond shape where it can best be seen.

fig.title: Daylight tow, under power
lines: Your stern to her stern: 220 m

q: You are writing the night orders for this tow. Which do you write?
a: A watch aft on the line, knife at hand; chafe and VHF checks hourly
o: Autopilot on; check the line at each change of watch
No one aft at night; her lights show she is still there
Check the line only if your speed over ground drops
why: A chafing or parted line is caught early only by someone watching it; hourly chafe and radio checks keep both crews on the same plan.

fig.title: Night tow, 12 h to port
lines: Crew of six on your yacht, two on the tow
VHF 72 and torch signals agreed
Towline: 100 m of nylon, chafe gear on

q: At 0300 the towline parts, and its end is trailing astern of your twin-screw yacht. What do you do first?
a: Both engines to neutral, then haul the line aboard
o: Turn back at once to pass her a new line
Speed up to keep the trailing line taut
Send a MAYDAY, as the tow is now adrift
why: A trailing line soon wraps a propeller and disables you too; stop the props, recover it, then plan the reconnection from upwind.

q: The yacht you are towing has lost her rudder and sheers 30° each way, snatching the line. What do you ask her crew to do?
a: Stream a drogue or a bight of warp from her stern
o: Shorten the towline to 20 m to hold her straight
Ask you to tow faster to straighten her out
Move the towline to one of her quarters
why: Drag astern of the tow acts like a tail and keeps her straight; a short line or more speed only makes each snatch harder.

fig.title: Tow without a rudder
lines: Towline 80 m, speed 4 kn
She sheers 30° each way
Line snatches at the end of each sheer

q: You are running your planing motor yacht before these seas. What do you do with the trim tabs?
a: Raise both tabs fully, so the bow rides higher
o: Lower both tabs fully, to hold the bow down
Lower the starboard tab only, against the yaw
Leave them: tabs change nothing at sea
why: Tabs down push the bow down — right in a head sea, wrong in a following one; raised, the bow stays up off the back of the wave ahead.

fig.title: 24 m planing yacht, 16 kn
lines: Seas F7 on the starboard quarter
Bow digs into the back of the wave ahead
She yaws hard each time it does

q: Could your displacement motor yacht keep pace with these seas and sit on the back of one?
a: No: the seas run at about 18 kn, she at about 11
o: Yes: the seas run at about 9 kn, she at about 11
No: the seas run at about 18 kn, she at about 6
Yes: the seas run at about 18 kn, she at about 22
why: 1.56 × 6 = 9.4 m/s ≈ 18 kn; 21.5 m = 70.5 ft, 1.34 × √70.5 ≈ 11 kn. She cannot keep up: slow down and let them pass under her.

fig.title: 24 m displacement yacht, following seas
lines: LWL 21.5 m; hull speed ≈ 1.34 × √LWL ft
Seas: period 6 s, deep water
Wave speed ≈ 1.56 × period m/s; 1 m/s = 1.94 kn

q: In following seas your twin-screw displacement yacht yaws to port as each crest lifts her stern. Which engine do you give a burst ahead to check it?
a: The port engine: its thrust swings the bow back to starboard
o: The starboard engine: its thrust pushes the bow to starboard
Both engines equally, to drive her straight on
The port engine astern, to pull the bow back round
why: Thrust ahead on the port side turns her to starboard about her centre; the port engine astern would turn her further to port.

fig.note: Twin screws · following seas · yawing to port

q: Your motor yacht lists to port in this beam wind. Which trim tab do you lower to level her?
a: The port tab, to lift the low side
o: The starboard tab, to push the high side down
Both tabs, by the same amount
Neither: tabs alter only the fore-and-aft trim
why: A lowered tab lifts the stern on its own side, so lowering the port tab raises the low port side and levels her.

fig.title: Beam wind, F6 from starboard
lines: She lists 4° to port at 18 kn
Both trim tabs now fully up

q: You must wait 8 hours for daylight off this harbour in your 24 m motor yacht. How do you ride out the gale?
a: Jog slowly head to sea, the seas fine on the bow
o: Stop the engines and drift beam-on to rest the crew
Run off downwind at speed and come back at dawn
Anchor off the entrance on all of the chain
why: A motor yacht cannot heave to; at steerage way head to sea she rides easily and holds her position, keeping her sea room.

fig.title: Off a harbour, gale SW 8
lines: Entrance breaking until daylight, 8 h
Sea room: 40 M to the NE
Crew of four, one seasick

q: Hove-to under the trysail, you see this. What do you change?
a: Move the sheet lead forward
o: Move the sheet lead further aft
Ease the sheet until the flutter stops
Sweat the halyard up harder
why: A lead further forward pulls the clew down as well as aft, tightening the leech and easing the foot, as with a jib.

The foot is bar-tight
Boom lashed down out of the way

q: You are about to hoist the trysail at the mast in a rising gale at night. How do you rig its sheets beforehand?
a: Two sheets, one to a block on each quarter, both led to winches
o: One sheet to the leeward quarter; rig the other after a tack
One sheet to the end of the boom, as for the mainsail
Two sheets, both led through the same quarter block
why: With both sheets led before the hoist, you can tack or change tack hove-to from the cockpit, and no one goes back to the clew.

q: You are running off and will stream your drogue astern. How much line do you give it?
a: About 115 m
o: About 76 m
About 38 m
About 16 m

fig.title: Running off under a drogue, F9

Want: drogue in a trough as she tops a crest,
and at least one wave length astern

q: The gale has passed, and you must recover the parachute sea anchor. How do you do it?
a: Motor up to its trip-line float and haul it in by the crown
o: Winch the rode in from the bow with the canopy still open
Cut it loose: a parachute cannot be recovered at sea
Haul in on the rode while motoring slowly away from it
why: Pulled by the crown on its trip line, the canopy spills its water and comes aboard easily; pulled by the rode, it holds tons of water.

q: You are hanking the storm jib on the inner forestay for a gale. Where do you set its tack?
a: On a pennant, so the foot sits well clear of the deck
o: Right down on the deck fitting, as low as it goes
Halfway up the stay, hoisted on a second halyard
Tied to the pulpit, so that it is easy to reach
why: Seas breaking over the foredeck fill a low-set storm jib and can tear it; a tack pennant lifts the foot clear of the water on deck.
